text: This is TALK OF THE NATION. I'm Lynn Neary in Washington.

Right now, circulation is down, jobs are being slashed, budgets are being squeezed and ad revenue is down - just another day in the life of the so-called traditional news media. But it turns out it's not all bad news for mainstream media. More people are actually reading newspapers; they're just doing it online. That's one of the findings in a new report out today by the Project for Excellence in Journalism. Tom Rosenstiel heads up the project and joins us here in Studio 3A to talk about this and other findings in his study.
Good to have you with us, Tom.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Hi. Thanks.

Well, we have been hearing for many years now that readership of newspapers is declining but your - this latest study, this latest in your annual reports on the state of the news media, seems to say it's a little more complex than that. Explain that.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Well, the audience is fragmenting across more platforms but it's not necessarily fragmenting across more news providers. I think a lot of people, five or six years ago, thought that the digital revolution was going to mean the end of the media oligarchy. The New York Times was going to lose its audience as it splintered away to hundreds of other places. And indeed, it's splintering across new technologies but now we've got enough information about where people are going - online.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: The top 10 newspaper Web sites, according to some research have 29 percent of the online newspaper audience. In print, the top 10 newspapers in the country have 19 percent of the print circulation. There's - by that measure and many others, a lot of reason to think that in the new technology, the old media are not losing their audience. It's just that the advertising is not migrating online to the new technology along with the audience, which is sticking with old media in a lot of ways.

And let me just remind our listeners that we are talking about the latest report and the state of news media for 2008, with Tom Rosenstiel, director of the Project for Excellence in Journalism. If you'd like to join the discussion, give us a call at 800-989-8255 or send us an e-mail to talk@npr.org.

What I found really interesting, Tom, especially if you've been looking at these reports over a period of time, is that what you found was that the newsroom is where the experimentation is taking place and its advertising that's falling behind and doesn't know quite how to deal with digital media.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Yeah, and that's related to the same phenomenon that the audience is sort of staying with old media in a lot of ways. Online, there is no full-page ad with lots and lots of information. Every ad is pretty small. Online, a newspaper needs to get in the TV ad business with video ads. Well, they don't have salespeople that know TV ads in the newspaper. And they don't have really print ad people at the TV station. So the newsroom is figuring out how can we give our print reporters a TV camera, how can we get give our radio reporters a digital camera to shoot video?

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: But it's actually turning out to be harder on the business side to figure out, well, all those clients you have that went away, you're going to have to find new clients to sell advertising to or maybe you're not going to sell advertising, maybe you're going to sell search. You're going to have to sell an entirely different product now. That's turning out to be harder than, okay, you told the story in audio, now tell it visually as well.
Yeah, and that's a problem for the news media, if the advertising part of - can't keep up with them then who's paying for what they're doing?

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Another way of looking at this is that the audience for The New York Times, what's produced by that newsroom is actually greater than it's ever been. And almost as most people go to The New York Times Web site now has read the paper in print. But The New York Times makes 93, roughly, 93 percent of its revenue from the print edition and only about 7 percent of its revenue online. So every time a reader shifts from a print reader to an online reader, it costs The New York Times money.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: So you also see that the business - that the newsrooms of newspapers across the country and to some extent, television stations. The news people are saying, well, let's figure out how we can monetize this. Let's figure out how we can sell the story. So the news people are getting more involved in the business thinking, and that wall…
Instead of go to the - yeah.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: …is sort of disappearing.
Well, is that a good or bad thing?

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Well, you know, that news people would say it's a good a thing as long as they're coming up with a business plan. I'm sure they'd say it would be a bad thing if the business people were kind of put the news plan.

Yeah. It's interesting, though, do you think that the news people - just because I've been covering these reports for a while, I feel like it sounds like this year you're saying there's been a turn in the mental - in the thinking of the news people that they've finally have come around instead of feeling like our industry is dead. They're saying, oh, it's not dead; it's just we have to look at it in a different way.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Yeah.
And that's a good thing.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Yes. I mean, we started this and you cover the first one in 2004 and at that point, we said, you know, there's very little innovation going on in traditional newsrooms online. I think they've moved from fear to anger to acceptance to, this year even, enthusiasm. And that's a real shift. I mean, just absolutely no question, you hear people saying - and we have a survey of journalists as part of the report - the majority of journalists say they think that journalist writing, blogs is good for journalism, that citizen news sites are good for journalism, that citizens posting comments on their stories are good for journalism and that splitting their time between their old platform and the new platform is a good thing rather than something that's spreading them thin. Those are findings I think would have meant just inconceivable three or four years ago.
Yeah.
If you'd like to join our discussion about the state of the news media, give us a call at 989-8255. I'm talking with Tom Rosenstiel, the director of the Project for Excellence in Journalism.

You know, some of the ways that - you were just talking about blogs, something else interesting in this report is that it turns out that some of these sort of user-generated sites are not going to play as bigger role as it was thought.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Yes. Two things about that struck me. One is that news people are saying, well, wait a second, it's fine to get tips from citizens and have them come in our stories but having them actually post content, we're finding it to be not as helpful as we thought. The other thing that we found that was interesting was when you go to the citizen news sites, they act very much like the old news sites.
Right, that was interesting.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: They don't let outsiders post original material other than commenting on their own stories. And the blogs are more like gatekeepers than the traditional media are. It's like this is my blog, it's not your blog. You can comment on my blog but I'm not letting - not handing it over to you.

Yeah. And let me ask our listeners, we want to post a question to you. How do you rate your newspaper as a news source? Where do you get your news from? And have you noticed that your local friendly blogger has become a gatekeeper?
Give us a call. The number is 800-989-8255.

Interesting, too, Tom, that you point out in this report that - and there's an understanding, I think, of this - in the newsroom as you say that there is no longer one single finished news product, that this a 24/7 service.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Yes. The idea that journalism is going from being a product to being a service, how can you help me? You know, it's - I go to your Web site at NPR and it's fine and you got your story there and that's a lovely story. But know I want to find out where else can I go and where can I buy this product, and how do I reach that person, and I'd like to suggest the next story to you, and by the way, let me tell you what I think of your story. It's really how can you help me as a news consumer rather than let me just read your stuff.
Yeah. Let's take a call now. We're going to go to Lenny(ph) and he is in Rochester, New York.
Hi Lenny.
Hi. Thanks for thanking my call.
You're welcome.

You know, I guess, my comment is that this political season, when I first started watching the news, you know, it was exciting just the in-depth coverage that you were getting. But quite frankly, it's been going on for so long that I've definitely hit the fatigue point. And, you know, I just don't want to watch the news anymore because it's more of the same thing or it's getting to the point where it almost begins to feel contrived and that the story, they're just keep digging and digging into the minutia of that - you kind of lose track of the big story with the political argument. I'm just fatigued with that aspect of journalism

Well, Tom, this is something that your report, in fact, does point out, which is that the news media, the agenda of a news media continues to sort of narrow rather than broaden, and I think you point out that Iraq and the campaign, I think, it was 25 percent of all the content in the news media was on Iraq and the campaign.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: In fact, if you were to take Iraq, Pakistan and Iran, those three countries, take them out of the mix and you take out hurricanes as sort of one-time events, that the entire rest of world made up less than 6 percent of all the news coverage that we monitored last year, and that includes Afghanistan and China.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: The problem here is as the financial pressure increases and your audience spreads across more platforms, you actually have fewer reporters at each outlet and everybody's cutting back, buying people out. And so you actually, even though there's more media, the number of reporters at anyone of those places is smaller, so their sort of peripheral vision is narrowed even though it seems like we have more media.

Tom Rosenstiel is the director of the Project of Excellence in Journalism. And we are talking about their annual report on the news media. The number if you would like to join us is 800-989-8255. And you are listening to TALK OF THE NATION from NPR News.
And we're going to take a call now from Chad(ph) in Jacksonville, Florida.
Hi Chad.
Hi. My name is Chad.
Go ahead.

I was just talking about - I get most of my media from either podcast or either the (unintelligible) online and I really like getting it from the Post online because it's almost like - it sort of like a Chinese menu. So I get to go in and pick what I want to both view the one (unintelligible) blog and a comment op-ed pieces with graphics, with videos and even with news that I feel like (unintelligible) thing or just like it's almost like I get a Chinese menu. That's how I kind of deal when I go to their Web site and I just think that's one of the best things about doing online news.
All right. Thanks so much for your call, Chad.
Thanks.
Tom?

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Yeah. Chad's absolutely right, I mean, the front page of a newspaper has about six stories on it. And the front page of a Web site has links to dozens and dozens of stories, and that notion is growing even more. I mean, the current thinking is that 50 percent of every Web page, even an interior page of a Web site, should be devoted to navigating to other things because there is no front page to a Web site anymore; you might enter from anywhere. And the net effect is that the power shifted to the consumer, to be their own navigator, to be their own editor.

And that means if somebody goes to the NPR Web site or The New York Times Web site, that they should be providing them with links to other Web sites. They shouldn't be worrying about those other Web sites being competition for them but that these are just links.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: A year ago, we saw - we did a big study of Web sites and found that most of the traditional Web sites are what we called walled gardens. They had only their own content. You got there and then you could look around NPR stuff. Today, that's - even a year later, not nearly so much the case as the editor of one major Web site told us, the walled garden is over. We have to be a portal to elsewhere as well as the stop along the way.
Okay. Let's take - we're going to take a call from Manuel(ph). He's calling from Florida.
Hi. Go ahead.
Hi. How are you?
Good.

Okay. I just wanted to make a comment. I'm a young visual journalist. I just got out of school about a year and a half ago. And one of the things that I found really fascinating about the newspaper industry now is that the younger generation is coming into the workplace with a lot of the new skills, new technology and have kind of a better understanding of the way that the Web is working and where it used to be, at least, I feel like in the newspaper industry, that experience is really what kind of pushed the newspaper industry forward. A lot of the younger generation are bringing new skills that are kind of hoping change the industry, and it's just an interesting paradigm that you have people with less experience but with more - a better understanding of the skills than what's needed to push the industry whereas the older generation is (unintelligible) kind of consult us on how the industry needs to go.
So you feel that some of the older generation of journalist you're working with are beginning to feel that they've got to learn this. Is that kind of what's happening?

Yeah. I mean, I don't want to sound, you know, like we're taking over the industry but I think it's interesting with this new technology particularly video and all the online efforts that are being done in the news industry, it's an incredible time for the younger generation to step in and help expand the platform and help push media in a new direction.
All right. Good point. I had to say, as a member of the news media, I think you might be right.
Well, it's great talking to you. It's my first time calling a radio station so I was a little nervous but thanks for having me.
You did very well. Thank you so much.
Take care.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: We hear the same thing from editors and by the way, they say, Manuel, it's also cost less to hire than the old guy or who doesn't have those skills.
And the other thing, what's really happening, you know, in real terms, is what he's pointing up is that everybody has to do more.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Yeah. And if you cannot adapt then you're an impediment to the newsroom which is trying desperately to figure out what's the potential of the new technology.

Yeah. Let me just ask one other question about the blogs you were saying, it's, you know, you were saying - I think your report is saying it's not playing a central role as you expected but it's still, people love to go to blogs and read blogs and, you know, if you're, for instance, I cover books, you know, I read the newspapers but I go to the - there's a whole - there's the literary blogs and then there's the economic blogs and people know where they want to go for their own blogs.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Yes, and people are using blogs but that not as a substitute to traditional media but as a complement. So that we're sort of that we're making room on the shelf for that.
All right. Tom, good talking to you about this again.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Thanks, Lynn.
We'll probably talk same time next year.
Tom Rosenstiel is the director of the Project for Excellence in Journalism. Their new report on the state of the news media is just out.
This is TALK OF THE NATION from NPR News. I'm Lynn Neary.

And today, we launch a new segment on Talk of the Nation. We call it A Question of Ethics. From time to time, we'll take an issue from the week's news and ask you to tell us what you would do if you were the reporter or the editor on that story. We'll talk about how the news media did cover the story, and we'll bring on an ethicist to discuss the choices and the issues.

This week, our question of ethics involves coverage of Senator Hillary Clinton's comment last week, when she brought up the assassination of Robert F. Kennedy. You've probably heard it by now, or heard about it. Senator Clinton was speaking to the editorial board of the Sioux Falls Argus-Leader in South Dakota. And while defending her decision to stay in the race, she said...
My husband did not wrap up the nomination in 1992 until he won the California primary somewhere in the middle of June, right? We all remember Bobby Kennedy was assassinated in June in California.

Did the news media handle that story responsibly? If you were in the editor's chair, would you have put her comments on the front page? Let us know why, or why not. 800-989-8255. Email us, talk@npr.org, and we'll also talk with members of the studio audience here at the Newseum. And you can join the conversation anytime on our blog. That's at npr.org/blogofthenation. Joining us today is Tom Rosenstiel, director of the Project for Excellence in Journalism, with us here at the Knight Studio in the Newseum. Tom, nice to have you back on the program.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Thanks, Neal.
And what exactly happened here? Put her comments into context for us.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Well, this was the first of three events that Mrs. Clinton was doing on Friday, and it was a meeting with the editorial board of this newspaper. And as several newspapers are now doing, they live-streamed this. They were videotaping it, and they live-streamed it over the Internet to any journalist who wanted to see it. And the press corps who travels with Mrs. Clinton were not there.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: They were actually traveling on a bus from the airport to Brandon, a few miles away, to set up her second event, which was at a supermarket. And they didn't see this. They really couldn't get a good feed. But the New York Post did an item on it online, which the Drudge Report then linked to. And their editors, back at their various headquarters, when they got to the supermarket, were saying, what about these comments? What about these comments?

And so therefore, then the story really took off. And it was a story, I guess, on its own for a couple of news cycles, first the story itself and then Senator Clinton's clarification of what she actually meant with these remarks. But it has been all over the blogs and the op-ed pages and the letters to the editor in the newspapers.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Yes. Now, before we say what happened, do we want to go and ask people what they would do? Or if you want to sort of tell the end of the story at the beginning?

Well, let's see what callers and members of the studio audience here at the Newseum would have done if they'd been presented with this story. And we have a caller on the line. This is Erin, Erin's with us from Cleveland, Ohio.
Hi.
Hi there.

I'm glad to get through, because this one got to me. I - for some reason, my husband and I are not Hillary supporters by any stretch of the imagination, but I just thought that it was so irresponsible, that it was so taken out of context and not at all what she meant.
Not at all that she meant that she was staying in the race in hopes, as...

In hopes, right, in hopes that Obama would be, you know, assassinated. It was just so outlandish to me, and something I never would have thought of if I had just heard her say it. So, it was real frustrating to me.
Tom Rosenstiel?

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Well, I guess the question is, would you put it in your story as a big deal? And where would you play that story?
I never would have even put it in the story, I don't think.
And would you have sent - or do you think your editor might be upset if it was in everybody else's story?
I would hope not, and if he were - if he or she were, I would find a new editor. I think the kind of editor I want to be...
Doesn't tend to work that way, I'm afraid.
Writing for. So, that's just my opinion, but that one got to me, just frustrating.
Erin, thanks very much.
Thank you.
So long. Let's see if we can try - this is Frank. Frank is on the line with us from Tallahassee in Florida.
Hey.
Hi there.

Hi. Yeah, I just think that a lot of the papers these days, the publications just do little things like that to sell magazines or sell newspapers and they don't tell the whole story, and I think it's a disservice to the American public. And that's why I think so many people listen to the NPR, because they tend to tell as much of the whole story as they can.
Thank you for the kind words, but in this context, what do you think the whole story was?
That - I don't know. To be honest, I don't know. It sounded like it was more confusion on her part or maybe the wrong words on her part.
In a 15-second Soundbite, and that's what everybody really did hear, with that conversation Tom Rosenstiel, you don't get a lot of context.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: No, and I think the fact that the reporters themselves who have traveled with Hillary Clinton weren't there as the first recipients of this, that they were actually reacting to their editors' reaction is a factor in how this played out, because their editors may have been unaware of the fact that she'd made references like this previously and it hit their radar differently.

So in other words, the reporters who were on the bus, as we were talking about earlier, they knew that Hillary Clinton had made references to the late decisions in 1968 and in 1992, maybe not using the word assassination, but this was not the first time she'd said that.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: And although she has made these references before, this was actually not the first time that she'd used the word assassination, although it came out a little differently this time.
Thanks so much for the call, Frank.
Sure. Have a good day.

And let's see if we can another opinion. This is Joe, Joe is with us from Cincinnati, Ohio. Joe, you're the reporter, you've seen this story as you've watched the streaming from the editorial board meeting, and what do you do with that story?

I think it's absolutely a front-page story. It's not about whether she hoped he would get assassinated. It's the mere fact that she decided that one of her rationales for staying in the race is that tragedy might befall her opponent, and she essentially evoked these very tragic memories as a justification for her to stay in the race.
And so you would put her on the front page? You would have led the story with it?
Definitely it was front-page news, there is no doubt about it.
Tom?

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Can I ask, Joe, a question? Does it make any difference if she didn't mean it that way? Does her intention make a difference? Or can it be construed the way that a lot of people construed it? Is that enough to make it a big story?

I guess you're asking me to try to guess what her intention is. My guess is that her intention was that. She is looking for every justification for her to stay in this race, and one of those justifications was, well, somebody might get assassinated or something bad might happen to them, but that's a good reason to stay in the race. And the way that these political campaigns are run, I find it difficult, and if you listen to her, she pauses right before she says it, it's almost as if she's thinking, should I really say this?
And if she has said, you know, my rival might be overtaken by scandal, how would that have figured into your thinking, Joe?
I don't know if that would be as strong of a front-page story, because scandal and assassination are two different things. I will leave it at that.
OK, thanks very much for the call, appreciate it. Let's see if we can get another caller in. This is Ian, Ian with us from Mililani - is that right?
Mililani, yes, that's right.
In Hawaii, go ahead, please.

Yeah, actually, I mean, I think that this - while I understand being streamed live it makes it sort of a temporary issue, the story really is just candidate sticks foot in mouth again, or candidate does something that looks inappropriate again. It's the way the press covers it after the fact, insinuating that, oh, what did she mean? That is a little disingenuous. It is the same thing that happened to Obama with the flag pin. It's like, oh, what does it mean that he wasn't wearing a flag pin or putting his hand over his heart?

It's not that she - I mean, nobody seriously thinks that she - actually, I disagree with the last caller who said they are justifying her staying in the race by invoking this idea that he might be assassinated, that she's explaining that things happen and there's every reason to stay in the race. She used a bad example. That she's insinuating something more sinister, I think that's baloney, same thing with the Obama and pin thing. It's just the way the media construes it after the fact. Thanks.

OK, Thanks very much for the call, Ian. Here's an email we have from Emily. I certainly would have put Hillary Clinton's comments on the front page if I were an editor of a major publication. She was speaking in front of cameras, knew that she was being recorded. If editors felt it appropriate to publish Obama's bitter comments, made in semi private, then I certainly feel that her comments were fair game. And again, she's referring to comments that Senator Obama made at a private fundraiser in San Francisco that were recorded by somebody in the room and then put out. This is where he said some small-town voters - I think he was talking about Pennsylvania - cling to guns and religion.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Yeah, and I think one of the things, one argument you can make is that, if you are going to be the leader of the United States, you need to speak with a kind of discipline where things cannot be taken out of context, where your meaning is clear, and if you invite through inference terrifying or awful implications or impression from what you're saying, you know, that's not a good thing for the leader of the free world to be doing.

An argument could be made, she's on the campaign trail. She's exhausted. Of course you're going to make mistakes. I think the job of president is also pretty exhausting and you could be pretty tired a lot of the time there, too.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Right, and there are a lot of people there who like to take things in a - put things in a context that's useful to them, in whatever you say.

We're talking with Tom Rosenstiel in A Question of Ethics. If you were an editor or a reporter on the story, when Hillary Clinton made those remarks in Sioux City, what would you do with them? Would you put them on the front page? Would you lead the story with them? You're listening to Talk of the Nation from NPR news. And Tom, let's talk for a minute about what the media actually did do with this story, and it was a pretty big deal.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Yeah, it became big instantly. That night, all three evening newscasts carried a story on it. It was the lead story on one of them and a second story on others. The main cable shows led with it in general. "Hardball" did its first three segments on it. Olbermann did four segments on it, including a commentary that was particularly caustic at the end of his show.
It's Keith Olbermann.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Keith Olbermann. Anderson Cooper did his first two segments on it. It was basically the lead story. Shepard Smith on Fox did his first two segments on it. But overall, in the amount of cable that we study each day, it made up 36 percent of the airtime on cable that night.
"We" is the Project for Excellence in Journalism.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Yes, and 12 percent of the nightly newscasts that evening. It was a front-page story in the New York Times, below the fold, below the midpoint of the newspaper. It was the lead story in the Washington Post the next day. And I think that context is everything. I think in politics, if you say something in February when you're potentially ahead, or it's a neck-and-neck race, it has one meaning.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: If you're at a point where many analysts believe you cannot win and the race is effectively over and you make the same remark as a justification for staying in the race, it can have a different meaning. I think it's quite possible that, had the reporters heard this first, this would not have been as big a story. But by the time reporters, the traveling reporters, become aware of it, the story had already taken on a life of its own through the Internet. It was in the blogosphere. People were commenting on it.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: There were actually comments and debates from readers of the New York Times on the New York Times website before the New York Times had posted a story about this event. And that's, as the Times reporter wrote the next day, it's a commentary, in a sense, on the media culture we have. The press, in some ways, was a reactor and not a gatekeeper to that story. And the people who wanted to seize on it seized on it before the reporters themselves who were traveling with her did.

In terms of news, it's a two-cycle story. The candidate makes the remark. The candidate clarifies the remark or retracts the remark, depending on what she has to call it. But it's been alive on the editorial pages, on the op-ed pages, and as you mentioned, on the blogosphere ever since.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: And she - interestingly, she had not spoke to her traveling press corps directly in a week, which is a commentary on the kind of atmosphere that was on that bus. She felt compelled, later that day, to address them, and she made a statement, did not take questions, in which she apologized for the remark. And that decision by her campaign that this thing had become a - had snowballed by midday, made it, in turn, a bigger story as you've said. The fact that she felt she'd made a mistake and apologized for it propelled the story onto page one and into the lead of the newscasts.
And what ethical issues do you see here for journalists?

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: Well, there's the question, first of all, of is it a story? There's the question of, what was her intention? And then there's the question of context. Ethically, you have to decide how big a story is something, how big a deal do I want to make of it? I'm not making the news, but I am making a judgment about how significant that news is. And the papers were saying, in a sense, regardless of what our reporters might have initially thought, or how they reacted to the same remarks two months earlier, this is now a big story, and it's a big story in part because of the anger in the Obama camp and the sense of tactical miscalculation in the Clinton camp.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: That gave the press, in a sense, a feeling that it was a bigger story. I think that the fact is that context matters, and had - these remarks do have a different connotation at a point in the race when she is perceived as not able to win. There's an old saying in politics that if you're ahead in the race and your campaign plane gets a flight tire on the runway, it's not a story.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism)
text: But in the TV era, that flat tire and that picture of your plane stuck on the tarmac is going to be the lead visual for the fact that you're the candidate behind in the race. And that's just sort of the reality of the way the media work now. I think the story was, in the end, overplayed. But I also think that it was, indeed, news in a way that it wasn't when the same remark was made two months ago.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism, Pew Research Center)
text: Well, it's that the audience for old media or traditional news values, the kinds of things that journalists have done for many, many years, continues to have an audience. That audience is often now migrating to the online version, but the old media are holding on to their audience.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism, Pew Research Center)
text: Well, many people predicted that, you know, once they could be rid of the annoying, obnoxious filters of old media...
Those terrible gatekeepers.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism, Pew Research Center)
text: And all of their fallacious ideas about objectivity and neutrality, that people would gravitate to other kinds of media and maybe just the media that they agreed with. speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism, Pew Research Center)

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism, Pew Research Center)
text: What has happened is something unexpected, which is that advertisers are not migrating to these old media Web sites along with the audience. The Internet has, in some ways, decoupled advertising from news, and so journalism's problem, as we've said here before, is more of a revenue problem.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism, Pew Research Center)

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism, Pew Research Center)
text: So even the people in network news, who have a much bigger audience than the cable news audience for any given program, say we're not competing against content, we're competing against a business model.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism, Pew Research Center)
text: Well, it's grown actually. I mean, we've seen some new media sites, you know, arrive at that, into the top 50 or top 20, but to put it this way, we looked at all 4,600 news and information Web site that Nielson Net Ratings tracks. The top seven percent of those, which is about 300 and something, get 80 percent of all the traffic, and if you go to the very top, the top 20, they get half of all that 80 percent of traffic.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism, Pew Research Center)
text: Now, who are those top 20? Well, they're either legacy media, like CBS News or ABC News or the New York Times, or they're aggregators like Yahoo who are aggregating old media. And at the same time, the revenue problems are not only severe, they're accelerating.

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism, Pew Research Center)

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism, Pew Research Center)
text: Right, if we can charge for this content, then it'll make a big difference. Other people, if you talk to executives at Google, they say you know what? That's not the way the Internet works. speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism, Pew Research Center)
text: So if you're reading a story about X, the ads that show up next to it are really specific, are geo-coded and coded with algorithms so that you know the people are going to be interested in that ad because of the story they're reading. speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism, Pew Research Center)
text: The other problem is that for newspapers in particular, most of what we thought of as classified advertising, which was the most profitable part of newspaper advertising...

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism, Pew Research Center)

J.R.: I used to sell advertising, both in print and radio. And my biggest piece and what I consider to be a part of the problem is, of course, it's always revenue. The number-one country - the number-one station in this market area is a country station. However, it's owned by a conglomerate - or a big, huge corporation that owns four or five other stations in the market area. They have one sales force or own stations. So the people are going out and selling 10 ads and putting two of them per station, so it doesn't work. Well, if doesn't work and I'm spending money for their advertising, I'm not going to advertise with them again.
He's...

J.R.: We have uneducated people. To me, part of the problem goes back to the FCC allowing the corporations to come in and buy up a marketplace, whether it be one or two in this particular area, we have three corporations that owned every media source, television stations, radio stations and print advertising...

And there are more than a few where one company owns all the radio stations in town. But Tom Rosenstiel, he's got a point. Lately, we've seen an uptick in ad revenue a bit. Do you think that's going to continue?

speaker_label: Mr. TOM ROSENSTIEL (Director, Project for Excellence in Journalism, Pew Research Center)
text: Well, I think it's going to continue as the economy improves. But I also think that the wave of consolidation that we began to see in the very late '90s and in the beginning of this decade came in at sort of exactly the wrong time, because the answer to fragmentation at that point was get bigger and economies of scale on the business side. Now we're in a new, you know, an entirely different world, where selling advertising to very small advertisers and selling a lot of it, the Google model, makes much more sense. That's the way the world is going: pennies per ad, a lot of ads, ads that are very highly targeted. And that's an extremely hard thing for the old, very large corporations that are consolidated to learn to do. They're about big clients and big accounts.

Again, if you got - like to take a look at this year's study on the State of the News Media from the Pew Research Center's Project for Excellence in Journalism, go to our Web site: npr.org.
